Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.

#6492. Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

While this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

But getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an important role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

Eagles appear to be hunting and killing adult baboons, study finds. Does that mean they could have hunted ancient human relatives?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eagles can hunt exceptionally large prey, including a baboon that weighed nearly 60 pounds (26 kilograms), a new study finds.

Some human ancestors were smaller in size than modern-day humans and weighed around the same amount as the baboons. This raises the question of whether they also might have faced eagle attacks, the researchers said.

Until now, it was thought that eagles couldn't lift nonhuman primates weighing over 29 pounds (13 kg), the researchers reported.

Scientists made the finding while conducting research in the Sahara Desert in Chad. They found the remains of at least nine adult baboons that had been killed recently by eagles. The region is home to Verreaux's eagles (Aquila verreauxii), which hunt from cliff tops, sometimes in pairs, and have talons with a grip diameter of 16 inches (40 centimeters). Grip diameter is how far the eagle’s grip extends.

The scientists found deep talon marks on the baboons' bones. These marks suggest that the eagles hunted and killed the primates and brought parts of them back to their nests, the team noted in a paper published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

The photo on the left shows an eagle-baboon encounter, while another image (right) features a baboon skeleton with marks of eagle predation.

The baboons were sizable, with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kilograms). The largest of them weighed 58 pounds (26 kg), which is similar in size to some small hominins, a group that includes humans and our close relatives that arose after the split from chimpanzees and bonobos, the researchers noted. For instance, the Australopithecus afarensis individual known as Lucy weighed about 62 pounds (28 kilograms) when she was alive in what is now Ethiopia around 3.2 million years ago.

While eagles do sometimes scavenge carcasses, this doesn't seem to be the case with the baboons. The "severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip," the team wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

They noted that eight out of nine of the baboons in the study were male. This suggests that the baboons were hunted, since scavenged animal remains would not favor a particular sex. Why eagles hunted mainly male baboons is not clear, and the "male sex-bias in our sample is puzzling," the researchers noted. Male primates, such as monkeys, do sometimes defend against eagles by charging at them, the team added in a statement.

There is one known example of eagles hunting and killing a hominin. The "only confirmed case is Taung Child, an infant Australopithecus who we think was taken by a large eagle around 2.8 million years ago," study first author Catherine Hobaiter, a professor at the University of St. Andrews in the U.K. who has studied primates extensively, told Live Science in an email. The Taung Child weighed around 22 pounds (10 kg).

Hobaiter noted that "several of the australopithecine species who lived around 1 [million to] 3 million years ago would be in the same weight range as the adult male baboons in our study" and would have been vulnerable to eagle attacks. Other large predators, such as hyenas and crocodiles, also would have been a threat.

Nowadays, smaller primates, such as monkeys, defend against eagle attacks by traveling together.

"Modern primate species that are predated by eagles spend time in mixed species groups — for example foraging together," Hobaiter said. "That means extra competition for the food — but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost."

Hominins may have done something similar, with different hominin species traveling together to defend against eagle attacks, she noted.

An illustration of a Verreaux's eagle hunting an adult male baboon.

Robert Simmons, a researcher at the FitzPatrick Institute of African Ornithology at the University of Cape Town who wasn't involved with the study, called the findings "fascinating." Eagles "are opportunistic — an old male or a young male baboon dispersing to another troop found on its own can become prey to an opportunistic eagle, or a pair of eagles," Simmons said in an email. In a desert region, the lack of cover can leave baboons exposed.

This is "certainly a rare occurrence," he said. But in this dry desert environment, the prey available to the Verreaux's eagles is limited, which has forced them to take on larger, more dangerous prey than is typical for a 9-pound (4 kg) eagle, Simmons explained.

W. Scott McGraw, an anthropology professor at The Ohio State University who also wasn't involved with the study, said in an email that early "hominins may have been particularly attractive targets because of their relatively small body size," especially infants and juveniles.

"Given their limited physical defenses, early hominins — and, indeed, primates more generally — likely evolved a range of behavioral adaptations to reduce their vulnerability to raptors and other predators," McGraw said. These adaptations may have included living in groups, yelling out to warn others, and selecting habitats that could offer protection from attacks.

Jesús Bautista-Rodríguez, the coordinator of the Desert Golden Eagles Project who has conducted extensive research on eagles, said that the finds were interesting but was cautious about some of the conclusions.

"I am much more cautious, however, about interpreting the remains described in this paper as evidence that the eagles actively killed healthy adult male baboons weighing over 20 kg [44 pounds]," Bautista-Rodriguez told Live Science in an email. "In my opinion, it is quite possible that some, or even all, of these individuals were already dead, dying, severely weakened or otherwise unable to defend themselves when the eagles fed on them."

He also took issue with how the baboons died, saying that more fieldwork is needed to better understand how eagles came across the baboons.

“The punctures and extensive scratches observed on the skulls and scapulae are certainly interesting and compatible with eagle talons and feeding activity," Bautista-Rodriguez said. "Nevertheless, these marks do not necessarily demonstrate that the eagle was responsible for killing the animal. They could also have been produced during the handling, dismemberment and feeding of an individual that had already died."

Hobaiter, C., Akpona, T.J.D., Kopp, G.H., Dominy, N.J. (2026). Signs of eagle predation on a 22-kg adult primate. American Journal of Biological Anthropology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.70377

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6488. Sheet-Pan Chicken Caesar Salad

This is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

Whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

#6487. We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

According to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

For gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

This is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

And if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

#6486. Million-Dollar Mac & Cheese

In my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

The cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

The combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That said, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

The crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

The gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

Storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.

Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly transform the brain — yet science is only beginning to understand how that transformation can affect a mother's mental health.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look closely at the medical illustrations used in textbooks to depict the physiological changes of pregnancy, and you'll notice something strange: The bodies often have no heads. Generations of physicians learned to picture the pregnant patient as a torso — a uterus, a placenta, a growing belly — with everything above the neck left blank.

That blank space is not an oversight by the illustrator. It is a faithful map of what medicine chose to study. We need to move on and create a complete picture of what happens during and after pregnancy so we can develop measures to prevent maternal deaths.

For hundreds of years, we have devoted enormous effort to characterizing how pregnancy remodels nearly every organ and system in the body: the cardiovascular changes, the recalibration of the immune system, the metabolic adjustments — most of them orchestrated by hormones the placenta pours into the bloodstream. That knowledge of what is normal is exactly what lets us recognize and treat what is not, from gestational diabetes to preeclampsia. But the brain, one of the most important organs in the human body, was left out altogether.

It wasn't until 2016 that my colleagues and I published the first study showing that pregnancy profoundly and measurably changes the structure of the human brain. That finding, which we described in the journal Nature Neuroscience, became the seed of my lab. In the years since, a remarkable picture has emerged. The brain changes associated with pregnancy and the postpartum phase are more pronounced, or at least occur more rapidly, than those of adolescence — the transformation we usually treat as the epitome of a remodeling brain.

Today, neuroscientists consider the months of pregnancy and the postpartum period to be one of the most plastic periods for the adult brain. These changes are dynamic; some regions shrink in volume during gestation and grow after birth, while others follow the opposite pattern. They are driven by hormones, tracking with the enormous swings in estrogens and other hormones across pregnancy. And they are long-lasting — some of these structural changes persist for years, and preliminary evidence suggests they may last decades. Or, as folk wisdom has long put it, once a mother, always a mother.

For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank.

These findings raise a question I'm asked constantly: Are these brain changes behind the phenomenon of "mommy brain," sometimes called "momnesia"? It is an effect many women report, and it deserves a careful accounting of its possible causes — among them sleep deprivation and the enormous mental and metabolic load of gestating and raising a human being. We are still investigating, but the data so far point in a reassuring direction: These brain changes are not associated with worse cognitive functioning. If anything, it's the opposite: We have evidence that the women whose brains changed the most were the ones who reported greater well-being and, in turn, an easier time bonding with their newborns.

But not every change is benign. The same plasticity that helps a mother adapt can also carry risk. In one of our most recent studies, published in the journal Science Advances in 2025, we found that certain brain changes were associated with a greater rise in depressive symptoms during the postpartum period. And here is the other side of the coin: A highly plastic brain is also a vulnerable one.

During pregnancy and the postpartum period, that same capacity for change makes the brain more susceptible to disturbances. The window that should lead to learning and bonding, for some women, opens onto suffering instead — especially when society fails to support them, when it doesn't recognize this period as a stage in which women need protection and support from their families and institutions.

The brain changes during pregnancy and the postpartum period are more pronounced and rapid than those that take place during adolescence.

The epidemiological data are as alarming as the personal stories behind them. Roughly 1 in 5 women will experience perinatal depression. In developed countries, suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. Let me say that again, because it bears repeating: Suicide linked to peripartum mental disorders is one of the leading causes of maternal death. And what happens to a mother's mental health does not stay with her — it ripples out to the well-being of her baby, her family and society as a whole. Advancing maternal mental health is urgent, and the first step is to generate the high-quality data that will let us truly understand the brain transformation that accompanies pregnancy and the postpartum period — to describe what happens to mothers on the basis of science, not personal opinion, inherited prejudice or incomplete medical models.

It is a serious problem, but the solution is straightforward ‪—‬ especially now, in the age of artificial intelligence. The tools of modern data science are extraordinarily powerful, but they are hungry ‪—‬ they need large, high-quality, deeply characterized datasets to learn from and make predictions. In maternal brain health, those datasets do not yet exist. We have blood biobanks from pregnancy, neuroimaging from postpartum parents, questionnaires on bonding, records on breastfeeding — but they sit in separate silos, captured at different moments, never integrated. No resource follows the same women from before conception, through pregnancy, and years past birth, linking biofluids, neuroimaging, neuropsychological assessments, and the social conditions of their lives.

Building that resource should be a priority for anyone who cares about women's health. It is the kind of infrastructure that transformed other fields. Databases like the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative for Alzheimer's disease and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study for adolescence turned scattered observations into predictive science. Motherhood deserves the same — not a footnote appended to the study of something else. It deserves its own chapter — its own public, longitudinal, well-characterized database, spanning from molecules to societies.

For the past nine years, my lab's efforts have focused on laying the groundwork for such a database, and we now have hundreds of participants assessed before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and in the postpartum period. But hundreds is not enough. To do this science properly, we need to scale from hundreds of women to thousands and to ensure, as much as possible, adequate geographic and social representation. My role within initiatives like ENIGMA-Neuroendocrinology and the Ann S. Bowers Women's Brain Health Initiative is to coordinate with other outstanding researchers to reach that goal with the highest quality and the greatest urgency we can manage.

None of this requires a scientific miracle. It requires a decision to treat the maternal brain as something worth studying with the same rigor and the same resources we devote to every other domain of biomedicine. For centuries, we drew the pregnant body without a head. We now have the tools to fill in what we left blank. What we need is the collective will, and the sustained funding, to finish the picture.

If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org.

Opinion on Live Science gives you insight on the most important issues in science that affect you and the world around you today, written by experts and leading scientists in their field.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

Eighty-five percent of women experience pregnancy at some point in their lives. It enables the very existence of our species. Yet this first step in the process of nurturing the next generation has had little serious, rigorous study — until now.

Susana Carmona's A Mother’s Brain is a landmark in ending sexual bias in women's health. Among her many initiatives, she is building a unique longitudinal database tracking how mothers’ brains change from preconception to several years after childbirth.

Susana Carmona is the author of "A Mother's Brain: The New Science of the Neuro-Maternal Revolution" (The MIT Press). Carmona is the founder of Neuromaternal, a lab based in Madrid, and is a mother herself. She has led international research projects and published her findings in Science Advances and Nature Neuroscience, among many other publications. Her research has been referenced across popular media from the CBS sitcom "The Big Bang Theory" to the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Washington Post, National Geographic, Smithsonian, and Mother Jones.

#6484. This Restaurant Chain Was Just Named America’s Favorite

This beloved American fast-food chain is known for its ButterBurgers and frozen custard. Can you guess?

Pop the cheese curds, Wisconsin! Forbes just released its first-ever America’s Favorite Restaurants list, and the No. 1 spot didn’t go to Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s or any coastal cult favorite (lookin’ at you, In-N-Out). It went to Culver’s.

To build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights company HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

The Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

We’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

The biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

#6483. Why Is Everyone So Obsessed With Protein?

Welcome to Gut Check, our column dedicated to the complex, ever-evolving relationship between food and our bodies. Whether you’re curious about mindful eating or want to understand what makes picky eaters picky, read on and let award-winning journalist Betsy Andrews answer all your burning questions.

I recently shed 20 pounds for my health, and I’m keeping it off by avoiding simple carbohydrates—pasta, pastries, white rice, most breads—and exercising with weights and resistance bands. Carbs make you feel full, at least temporarily, and without them, especially when I’m hungry after a workout, I’m turning to an even more filling macronutrient: protein. I’m 63, and my wife is 60. We’ve heard that dietary protein is key to wellness in aging. But, after recent blood work, she is worrying about “bad,” or LDL, cholesterol. All this leaves me pondering the types and amounts of proteins I should be cooking that won’t increase her cholesterol levels or my waistline but will make for satisfying, healthy meals.

In my current obsession with protein, I’m not alone. Americans are bingeing on the stuff: Social media is glutted with influencers promoting protein powders and heavy meat consumption; supermarket shelves have filled with packaged snacks advertising excess protein; and restaurants are overhauling menus to feed the needs of protein-hungry diners. Even the new USDA dietary guidelines encourage protein uptake. At its extreme, it’s a trend known as protein-maxxing, and everyone from the Kardashians to the American Medical Association is talking about it.

Our bodies need protein to function. “Protein is made of amino acids. When we digest protein, we release those amino acids and use them to build and maintain our own proteins: muscle, liver, heart, lungs, and even some bone,” explains kinesiology professor Stuart Phillips, director of the Physical Activity Centre of Excellence (PACE) at Ontario’s McMaster University in Canada. “Protein supplies materials for enzymes, antibodies, transport proteins, some hormones, and the repair of tissues and organs.”

Of the 20 amino acids in our bodies, nine are essential, meaning we can’t create them ourselves. We must get them from eating protein, and we need to keep up protein consumption, because our bodies deplete it as we digest it. “The simple takeaway is that protein builds you from the inside out. It is foundational,” says dietitian Daphene Altema-Johnson, senior program officer at the Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future. “But unlike fat, your body doesn’t have a dedicated storage system for protein, so you need a steady supply from food.”

In a culture built on body image, protein is also touted for its body-sculpting and weight-loss benefits. “You use protein to help build and maintain muscle mass and also recover from a workout,” explains Zach Rocheleau, the creator of the protein-rich recipes that comprise The Flexible Dieting Lifestyle. “It’s also the most satiating macronutrient. Getting the satiety effects of protein and thus feeling full, so eating less calories, is the driver that goes into losing weight.”

When influencers like Rocheleau claim that the protein they’re eating has helped them shape their physique, they aren’t wrong. Research does show that if you eat more protein it assists (to a point) in building lean muscle mass during resistance training. And studies have established the relationship between protein consumption, satiation, and weight loss. “The hype has come from real physiological needs,” says Dr. Megan Rossi, founder of The Gut Health Doctor, “but it’s more of an aesthetic effect, where people associate protein with big muscles and think the more protein they eat, the bulkier they’ll get.”

Scarfing down cheeseburgers and looking great doing it sounds good, but eating too much protein can put stress on your body, especially the kidneys. When you eat protein, Altema-Johnson explains, “The nitrogen part of it is stripped off and converted to urea, which is filtered out by your kidneys. Lots of nitrogen waste leads to a chronically higher kidney workload.”

For most people, this shouldn’t be much to worry about: Though he notes that this isn’t an endorsement of long-term protein bingeing, Phillips’ meta-analysis found no negative effect of higher protein consumption on kidney function in healthy adults. But if your kidneys aren’t in tip-top shape, stressing them can contribute to high blood pressure and other heart conditions. And studies show that consume excess animal-based proteins, in particular, can increase the risk of kidney stones.

There’s another potential problem: Your small intestine can only digest so much protein, so in high amounts, some of it ends up in your colon, where it can produce potentially harmful by-products. “Excess protein, like poorly absorbed egg whites and red meat, can ferment and produce toxic metabolites, which are associated with heart disease,” says Rossi. The solution is to eat fiber as well. But when you’re protein-maxxing, other nutrients, including fiber, can fall to the wayside.

Finally, though protein-maxxing is often touted as a way to slim down, the opposite can be true, too. “Your body has a ceiling for how much protein you can use,” says Altema-Johnson. Excess protein gets converted into glucose or fat for energy. Calories are energy units. You only need so many of them, and if you’re “chasing a protein number instead of eating until full,” as Altema-Johnson puts it, studies show that the extra calories can lead to weight gain.

Some protein-enriched packaged foods harbor sneaky calories. According to Rocheleau—who, by the way, eschews the phrase “protein-maxxing” in his work—“You would think that somebody putting out a high-protein product would take calories from carbs and fats and replace them with protein, but generally they keep the product the same but add protein, so you’re getting a lot more calories.” Plus, the marketing of protein-added snacks actually creates an insidious halo effect. “If you slap ‘high protein’ on a package, there’s the perception that it is automatically healthy, which can lead to overconsumption,” says Altema-Johnson. And while dairy- or plant-based protein products, including powdered supplements, can be a convenient way to support higher training needs to fill a genuine gap in the diet, Phillips’ research shows that they’re not a substitute for exercise itself and that protein intake had diminishing gains over a certain amount.

So what is the optimum amount of protein we should consume? Guidelines differ. Like the USDA previously, Canadian guidelines suggest a daily protein intake of .8 grams per kilogram of body weight. (To convert your body weight from pounds to kilograms, just divide it by 2.2.) For me, at 77 kilograms, 62 grams of protein per day is a good target, according to these guidelines, which comes out to a little over 8 ounces of roast chicken to meet my goals for the day. U.K. guidelines recommend slightly less, at .75 grams per kilogram, while the new USDA guidelines have been cranked up to 1.2 to 1.6 grams. At that serving goal, I can scarf down more than a pound of roast bird a day, and in theory, that’s what experts want me to do. For active and older adults, Phillips likes the new USDA targets, because we lose muscle mass as we age, and we start to need more protein to help retain it.

But not all protein is created equal. With my partner’s concern over cholesterol, maybe a skin-on bird dripping fat or a well-marbled steak seared in butter, both high in saturated fat, isn’t optimal for us. “This is where individualization matters,” says Altema-Johnson. “The goal is not zero red meat, but smaller proportions, moderation, and smarter cuts.” Experts like her, and plenty of studies, will warn you away from fattier and, especially, processed meats. “Unprocessed steak, ground beef, even pork chops have a modest health-associated risk,” Altema-Johnson says. “But bacon, sausage, deli meat, hot dogs—if you’re eating those constantly, you’re at higher risk for heart disease, colorectal cancer, and other health issues.”

Unlike animal proteins, not all plants contain every amino acid that our bodies need. But you can combine various vegetable proteins to meet those goals. Phillips and his colleagues found that young vegan and omnivorous men eating around 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day achieved similar muscle and strength gains with resistance training. “Grains tend to be relatively low in lysine. Legumes help address that limitation, while grains complement legumes’ amino acid profiles,” he says. “Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh, edamame, eggs, milk, yogurt, nuts, and seeds can all contribute. Soy is a particularly useful plant protein.” You don’t have to mix and match them at every meal, but a diverse plant-based diet can bring the protein you need.

The biggest takeaway is that you can’t just protein-max in the absence of overall healthy lifestyle choices. One of those is a balanced diet. According to Altema-Johnson, we should “individualize, moderate and balance. It’s important to have a diverse plate. If you’re focusing on one type of protein, especially meat, you’re missing out on all the good yummies a body needs.”

Chief among those yummies is fiber. Rossi says that recent studies support the idea that increasing protein can have benefits for weight-lifting and even aging, “but you need to increase fiber to balance it so your microbiome has more to eat than just excess protein. We need to swing the fiber flag.” Another recent study showed that 93 percent of Americans get enough protein, but other research reveals the opposite for fiber: Just 7 percent of us eat an adequate amount. That’s not good. A review of more than 5,000 studies found that a diet low in red meat but high in fiber-rich whole grains, vegetables, and nuts lowered our risk of death due to heart disease. “For gut health,” Phillips says, we should “ask what your protein habit is pushing off the plate.”

The other important lifestyle choice is exercise. “You can’t just expect to be sitting on the couch and eating protein and having these huge gains. Physical activity and resistance training bring far bigger results,” Rossi notes. That’s why I’ve ultimately been committed to moving more: Preventing muscle loss is insurance for my future. “Without enough protein and—most importantly, in my opinion—resistance exercise, this loss speeds up significantly,” says Altema-Johnson. “It affects strength, ability, balance, and fall risk. Muscle loss is directly tied to independence. It’s the difference between carrying your own groceries at 80 or needing help.”

Of course, I’m getting a late start. “You do not wake up at 65 with a new protein requirement. Start paying attention in midlife (over 40), and pair the protein with strength training, as that is the big lever to promote health, not protein,” notes Phillips. Well, I’m not 65 yet, but I did almost hit that age without addressing these health needs. Now I know that I need to exercise, and to support the training, I need a bit more protein, but not piles of it, and it has to come from a variety of sources. Perhaps most importantly, I’ll continue to take whatever the trend-setters are pushing on the socials with a grain of salt. As Phillips puts it, “Protein is a nutrient, not an identity. The goal is enough to support health, not as much as you can eat.”

#6482. 57 Food Gifts We’re Giving (and Secretly Hoping to Get) in 2026

It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting. After all, getting your shopping done now means you can focus on the important things once the holidays actually roll around—you know, like spending time with family, cooking a festive feast, and enjoying plenty of mulled cider and wine. If you’re in need of gifts for the food people in your life, look no further. These are the 57 gifts we’re planning to give (or hoping to receive) this year.

A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!). Tailor your pick to your giftee’s caffeine preferences to make it feel more personal: opt for an oversized mug for the friend who needs drip coffee on an IV, or a more petite cup for the cappuccino drinker.

I recently added these elegant tumblers to my collection thinking they’d be great for dinner parties, and they are—but they’ve also become my new favorite everyday water and iced latte glasses, because while they’re beautiful, they feel sturdy enough for daily use. They bring a smile to my face every time I use them, which is exactly what a great gift should do, isn’t it?

An olive oil can is the kind of thing that’s meant to live on your counter, so why not upgrade to a beautiful one? This sleek stainless-steel model from Seattle-based design studio Holcomb has been in my gifting rotation since it was released. It goes with multiple different home aesthetics and looks equally at home by the stove as it does on a dinner party table.

Give the designated host friend a set of whimsical spiral-tipped serving utensils to use at their next dinner party. And don’t worry, they’re dishwasher-safe.

Buttered toast is a perfect food, in my opinion, and anyone that agrees will adore this handblown glass butter keeper from East Fork. Its design ensures your butter can be kept at room temperature for weeks without spoiling, which means it’ll stay perfectly spreadable and ready to be swiped across whatever carbs you choose.

Any friend who cooks will appreciate receiving this set of ramekins from cult-favorite pottery brand East Fork. At four ounces, they’re a versatile size that works for equally as well for portioning mise en place as it does for serving condiments or sauces.

This stylish pepper grinder looks incredibly cool, but it’s also made with function in mind. That swanky-looking handle? It’s designed to be ergonomic, able to be held and twisted in myriad ways depending on what’s most comfortable for the user. This gift set pairs the grinder with Piper’s 50-50 blend of black and red peppercorns, portioned into four individual packets to ensure the spices stay fresh.

These stunning wood cutting boards are truly heirloom-worthy, handcrafted by expert woodworkers from sturdy hardwood. They’re versatile pieces that are durable enough to be your everyday chopping boards and beautiful enough to serve as serving vessels for cheese and charcuterie.

You can’t go wrong with a beautiful vase, especially if you fill that vase with a bouquet of fresh flowers. This colorful glass number is sure to earn your giftee compliments, and I love that it’s hand-blown, which means every piece is one-of-a-kind.

You never know when you need a large bowl until you find yourself in need of a large bowl. Any person who likes to host should have a few attractive options on hand, and a splatter enamelware bowl is a pretty timeless choice.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

Get the friend who nerds out on coffee roasting and fermentation processes a subscription to Podium Coffee Club’s Platinum tier, which sources its monthly beans from award-winning roasters across the country. The Platinum tier is focused on rare coffee varietals made using experimental techniques, so it’s perfect for someone who likes an expressive, unique roast.

This gift set brings a taste of Richard Christiansen’s Flamingo Estate to your pantry. It’s full of high-quality products you’ll actually use—no weird spice blends or waxy chocolates here.

For the friend who would gladly eat tinned fish for dinner every night, I suggest this 10-pack of greatest hits from Fishwife. It’s got a little bit of everything, from the brand’s smoked salmon collab with Fly By Jing to the fan-favorite Smoked Rainbow Trout with Chimichurri, plus limited edition Little Sardines, which are available only as a part of holiday sets.

We all know someone who finishes every dish with flaky salt. Get them this pack of tins from Jacobsen Salt Co., each of which is filled with a different kind of infused salt. They’re small enough to slip into even the tiniest of purses, so your salt-loving friend will never be without their favorite flaky finisher.

When in doubt, opt for wine. But instead of picking up a random bottle, treat your giftee to a month (or three or six!) of deliveries from New York City wine bar and shop Parcelle, whose Wine Drop subscription service has been a longtime BA fave. Choose between red, white, rare, or a curated monthly mix, and Parcelle will take care of the rest.

If you know somebody with a matcha habit that’s burning a hole through their wallet, they’d probably appreciate a set of ceremonial-grade powders from a tried-and-true brand like Matchaful. This set is also perfect for demonstrating just how different matcha powders can be.

This snazzy supply of olive oil is a great example of a practical item that’s still gift-worthy. The bold tin (designed in collaboration with Los Angeles–based artist Dave Bowers) makes it a statement kitchen decor piece, and the oil inside is cold-pressed in California by one of our favorite olive oil brands.

Diaspora Spice Co. spices are nothing like the bottles you'd find at the grocery store. Do a side by side smell test and the difference will be obvious to you. Diaspora’s product offerings have expanded quite a bit since it first got going. If the choices are overwhelming, the brand’s gift sets, like this one assembled by the one and only Padma Lakshmi, is a no-fail choice.

Balsamic Vinegar of Modena & White Condiment Set

Not all balsamic vinegars are created equally. Giusti is one of the oldest names in the business, and its vinegars are truly exceptional. The three medal is the brand’s most popular bottle, striking an ideal balance between sweetness and acidity. The white condiment is light and zippy and, honestly, good enough to drink.

This marmalade is the closest thing you can get to spreading Ojai, California on your morning toast. The flavors aren’t typical of marmalades you’d find in the store, the brand accents that bittersweet citrus zing with hibiscus and honey. Their fruit spreads are fantastic too.

You'd be pretty hard-pressed to find a cast-iron skillet like the Field No.5. Its sloped edges make tossing and flipping ingredients like a chef very easy, something you most definitely can’t do with your standard Lodge. Senior editor Olivia Tarantino uses hers every time she makes eggs.

Fellow’s full suite of cocktail-making tools looks like they’d fit right in among the equipment inside a spaceship laboratory (in the best possible way). It includes a jigger, a glass mixing vessel, a cocktail shaker, two strainers, a muddler, a bar spoon, and a tray to keep it all together.

Food storage is about as practical as gifts get, but Misenware makes it feel special. Our testing samples vanished from the BA office almost instantly, and plenty of staffers bought their own once we had run out. The stainless-steel containers seal so tightly that we have no fear of soup leaking in a work bag. They’re microwave-safe, they won’t stain, and they held up when we jumped up and down on them. A universal lid fits every size, and each piece nests inside the next. This Gear of the Year winner has never been on sale, so grab a set to give and another to keep while it's 25% off.

These cheery yellow kitchen scissors aren’t just fun to look at—they’re super practical too. The shears come equipped with a bottle opener, a nutcracker, and a lid opener, and the blades separate for easy cleaning, plus the bright color makes them easy to spot amid all your other cooking tools.

That aunt who always insists on baking the pies for Thanksgiving? Get her a handmade walnut rolling pin she’ll use for years to come. These French-style pins come in a marbled cardboard case that’s perfect for gifting. Their handleless design makes them comfortable to grip and easy to maneuver, and allows you to get a nuanced feel for your dough as you roll.

These adorable scrubbers are great for cleaning grime off delicate cookware, dishes, or glassware. They’re absorbent and fast-drying, and they have hooks for hanging—plus they’re incredibly cute.

This tortoise-handled bottle opener from Parisian flatware brand Sabre makes for a handsome host gift, especially when paired with a bottle of your favorite pét-nat or non-alc apéritif.

I’m secretly hoping someone restocks my own supply of this luxurious hand wash this holiday season. It comes in a glass bottle that’s so pretty I took to refilling it with cheaper hand soap after the original soap was long gone, but the scent—a delicate mix of jasmine, geranium, and orange blossom—is what really makes it worth buying.

These all-natural firestarters are a chic alternative to the typical firestarter logs, and they’d make an excellent host gift for the friend who’s lucky enough to have a fireplace or outdoor fire pit.

Give the gift of cozy hot pot nights at home with this cute and compact appliance by Fly By Jing. You could even pair it with an H Mart gift card so your giftee can stock up on thinly sliced meats and other add-ins.

The iced beverage fiend in your life will go gaga for this mini version of our longtime favorite ice maker, the GE Opal. Despite its more compact footprint and lower price tag, it produces the same crunchy nugget ice we know and love—and it’s available in some cute colorways.

Give the latte lover who also values convenience this do-it-all machine from Nespresso, which combines the brand’s signature pod technology with an automatic milk frother that’ll have them pouring latte art like a pro.

Cookbooks make for great gifts, and lucky for you, we’ve spent all year cooking through dozens of them to find the best ones. These are a few favorites from our quarterly best new releases roundups, like Yotam Ottolenghi’s latest collection of weeknight-friendly recipes and Roxana Jullapat’s ode to morning baking.

Obsessed With the Best: 100+ Methodically Perfected Recipes Based on 20+ Head-to-Head Tests

Ohana Style: Food from Hawai'i, for Your Family

No. 1 Best Indian Cookbook in the World: At-Home Recipes from the Streets, Truck Stops, Villages, and Palaces of India

Hello, Home Cooking: Do-Able Dishes for Every Day

Morning Baker: Recipes and Rituals for Breakfast and Beyond

Former BA staffer Ali Francis teamed up with illustrator Adriana Picker to create a truly one-of-a-kind book about the fascinating histories of vegetables. It’s truly a gem to behold, and the sort of book any cooking enthusiast would find joy in. Also, each year Phaidon issues a spectacular array of beautifully crafted and often massive cookbooks and tomes on food.

The Curious Lives of Vegetables: An Artful Exploration of the Wonderful World of Edible Plants, Their History, and Their Crucial Role in Our Future by Ali Francis

Le Cordon Bleu Culinary Arts School: Volumes 1-7 by André Cointreau

The Festive Baker: A Cookbook - Baking for celebrations and special occasions around the world by Ben Mervis

The Photographer's Cookbook by Lisa Hostetler

We are in the midst of a merch renaissance. Cult-favorite food brands and restaurants alike are selling all manner of hats, sweatshirts, T-shirts, and socks with their own signature visual aesthetics. Below are some selects from some brands you might recognize—like Fly By Jing and Fishwife—as well as some picks from BA staffers from their favorite restaurant spots around the country.

A factory worker experimented with a pressurized air system while on the job, and it resulted in a fatal injury.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 35-year-old man in the Czech Republic

The symptoms: The man was injured while working in a factory. His co-workers learned he'd been hurt after he crawled from the ground floor to the first floor and shouted for help. He had severe abdominal pain and rectal bleeding, and he said he had been injured while conducting "a silly experiment" involving a pressurized air system. However, he did not describe exactly what had happened.

"He repeatedly stressed that the incident was his own fault," doctors later wrote in a report of his case.

What happened next: The man was flown by helicopter to a nearby hospital, but during the flight, he became unresponsive and showed signs of hemorrhagic shock — a type of shock caused by significant blood loss over a short period. Shock, broadly, is when organs and body tissues don't receive enough oxygen due to decreased blood flow; if untreated, it can lead to organ failure and death.

Medical attendants in the helicopter worked to revive the man, but he died before he could be admitted to the hospital. Because the fatal injury occurred at the man's workplace, the police ordered a medicolegal autopsy, which both identifies the cause of death and collects details for law enforcement agencies, as part of an inquest procedure.

The autopsy: The coroner examined the body and noted that the soft tissues of the man's face were swollen and abnormally distended from retained air. The man's anus and genital areas were similarly distended and densely coated with dried blood, with radial tears in the skin surrounding the anus.

Next, the coroner conducted an internal examination. The man's brain was swollen, and he had air bubbles in his brain and chest cavity. Blood had collected around his diaphragm (the large muscle that helps inflate and deflate the lungs). It had also accumulated in the wall between the heart chambers on the left side, in tubes leading to his lungs, and in the membranes covering his lungs and heart. Reservoirs of blood also pooled in the man's abdominal cavity, in the tube leading to his right kidney, and in his digestive organs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The man's heart was "shrunken and empty," according to the report.

The autopsy also revealed foreign objects stuck between loops of the man's small intestine. These included three pieces of a black rubber pipe stopper and scraps of a plastic bag. His rectum — the final straight portion of the large intestine — had detached violently from his anus. It was surrounded by blood and marked with a laceration that was nearly circular, indicating that an "explosive rectal injury" had triggered hemorrhagic shock and caused the man's death, the coroner concluded.

Further investigation: Additional evidence from the factory and rubber fragments in the man's small intestine provided the police with further insight into his injuries; additional clues came from his internet search history, including photos of himself that he'd submitted to an amateur sex website.

The police concluded that the man had been performing autoerotic anal stimulation while at work, using a rubber inflatable pipe stopper measuring 2 to 3 inches (50 to 70 millimeters) in diameter, and an air gun, a handheld device for directing powerful jets of compressed air.

They suggested that the man likely attached the expandable pipe stopper to the muzzle of the air gun, which was in turn connected to the factory's air distribution system by a long, high-pressure hose. He then covered the pipe stopper with a plastic bag, inserted it into his rectal cavity, and pressed the air gun's trigger, causing "an unexpected abrupt inflation and explosive bursting of the pipe stopper within his rectum," the doctors wrote in the case report.

What makes the case unique: This case is the first recorded example of a person dying from a "rectal explosion during self-gratification," the doctors wrote. Piecing together the circumstances leading up to the man's injury was important for the hospital's doctors and law enforcement to understand how the fatality likely occurred, the authors said.

When performed responsibly and consensually, rectal insertion of foreign bodies typically does not cause significant injury, the authors added. However, "the introduction of some objects into the rectum might have unpredictable and even fatal effects."

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Hejna, P., Zátopková, L., & Janík, M. (2020). Rectal explosion: A strange case of autoerotic death. International Journal of Legal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00414-020-02344-7

#6479. The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director

#6478. Our 20 Favorite Canned Tomato Recipes

There are certain foods that we wish we could package up and save forever, and tomatoes are at the top of that list. Canning is an excellent way to hold onto the fleeting abundance of summer, when these versatile fruits are at their ripest, juiciest, and most flavorful. Canning may never be able to re-create the feeling of picking a plump, juicy tomato fresh from the vine and slicing it while it’s still warm from the sun, but in the depths of winter, we’ll take what we can get. Whether they are using diced, puréed, crushed, or whole canned tomatoes, these recipes make the most of the ingredient, extending its life well beyond the growing season.

This classic sauce from Bolognese cooking teachers Margherita and Valeria Simili combines ground beef with prosciutto, chicken livers, milk, and tomato purée. The slow-simmered sauce is a natural partner for serving over pasta or as a hearty filling for lasagna. Get the recipe >

Stalks of crisp celery are cut into bite-size pieces and slowly braised with tomatoes, onion, prosciutto, and olive oil until tender. This simple Italian preparation transforms a vegetable that’s often an afterthought into a comforting side dish. Get the recipe >

Agrodolce, or “sour and sweet” in Italian, is a classic Sicilian sauce, here paired with tender steamed broccoli. Red wine, canned tomatoes, vinegar, raisins, and black olives give the sauce its characteristic sweet-tart and slightly salty balance, while toasted pine nuts add a little crunch. Get the recipe >

In this simple recipe, beef short ribs slowly braise with red wine, garlic, onion, and canned tomatoes until the meat is fall-apart tender. It’s a hearty, straightforward one-pot meal that makes especially good use of pantry staples. Get the recipe >

This stuffed pasta with ridged edges from celebrated Los Angeles chef Evan Funke pairs a filling of ricotta and greens with a humble lightly cooked tomato sauce. Get the recipe >

This classic Sicilian dish balances tender fried eggplant with caramelized onions, golden raisins, olives, capers, and a sweet-tart tomato sauce. An unexpected addition of unsweetened chocolate brings a subtle bitterness that rounds out the sweet and savory flavors. Get the recipe >

While not the pizza that many people think of, this beloved Rhode Island specialty features thick, airy rectangles of focaccia-like dough topped with a simple tomato sauce. Traditionally served at room temperature, they’re a fixture at bakeries, parties, and family gatherings. Get the recipe >

Lamb, torn pita, and herbs are formed into tender rounds and simmered in a spicy tomato sauce, then finished with a cool, lemony aioli. The dish can be prepared ahead and reheated before serving, with the greens and sauce added at the last minute. Get the recipe >

A tomato-packed broth made with topneck clams and salt pork provides the foundation for this hearty soup. The mixture is chilled overnight, giving the flavors time to meld before being finished with bacon, onion, celery, garlic, and fresh herbs. Get the recipe >

Roasted pumpkin, winter squash, sweet potato, and bell pepper are folded into a tomato-based sauce spiced with cumin, coriander, and harissa. Chickpeas and dried apricots make the stew hearty and subtly sweet, while bulgur mixed with dried cherries and raisins makes for a flavorful, filling base. Get the recipe >

These crisp, golden fritters bring together tender Sea Island red peas, Carolina Gold rice, and collard greens in a nod to the flavors of South Carolina’s Lowcountry. The accompanying sauce simmers canned tomatoes with brown sugar, cider vinegar, and smoked paprika, creating a bright, tangy dip with just a hint of sweetness and smoke. Get the recipe >

This Sicilian baked pasta layers ring-shaped noodles with a tomato-rich ragù of beef, pork, and peas, plus fried eggplant, hard-boiled eggs, ham, and cheese. It’s the kind of deeply layered, all-in-one dish that makes for the perfect centerpiece when cooking for a crowd. Get the recipe >

This Roman classic gets its character from slow-braised oxtail and an unusually simple combination of tomatoes and celery, with no garlic or onions. The sauce is even better made a day or two ahead, giving the flavors time to deepen before it’s tossed with the cooked pasta. Get the recipe >

Creamy polenta provides the filling backbone of this dish, while sausage stewed in marinara sauce brings a rich, savory depth. Finished with grated Pecorino Romano, it’s a classic Italian comfort food that’s hearty, satisfying, and perfect for a cozy dinner. Get the recipe >

This cultural mash-up pairs chewy udon noodles with a deeply savory tomato sauce spiked with guanciale, white miso, chile, and Pecorino Romano. The sauce starts with canned San Marzano tomatoes, which simmer with garlic and onion until thick and rich. Get the recipe >

This southern Italian dish from famed cookbook author Marcella Hazan pairs seared lamb chops with a simple skillet sauce of canned San Marzano tomatoes, sweet red peppers, green olives, onion, and parsley. The chops finish in the sauce, picking up its savory, briny flavor. Get the recipe >

Fresh chiles are cooked alongside onions, garlic, and spices, providing an aromatic base for the sauce of crushed tomatoes. Eggs provide a hit of protein and a richness to counteract the sauce’s heat and acidity, while a sprinkling of feta cheese and chopped parsley add a touch of saltiness and verdant freshness. Get the recipe >

A year-round take on a classic Italian summer salad, this version uses canned tomatoes to soak into dry country bread, along with roasted fennel, fresh mozzarella, peppery arugula, and bitter radicchio. Get the recipe >

Marcella Hazan’s classic tomato sauce proves that great Italian cooking doesn’t need to be complicated. Canned tomatoes simmer gently with butter and onion, creating a rich, silky sauce with remarkable depth and a subtle sweetness. The result is a simple sauce that lets the quality of its few ingredients shine. Get the recipe >
