#6413. This 3D-Printed Robot Runs, Swims, and Climbs Without Any Electronics

A robot powered entirely by air could offer a new way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.

A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10.6 miles per hour (4.72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.

Built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego, the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim. Perhaps most remarkably, the entire robot is 3D-printed in one piece using a single material, and it needs no electronics to move.

The breakthrough, described in Science Robotics, takes inspiration from a centuries-old invention, the steam engine. By adapting the way steam engines make efficient use of pressure, researchers found a way to make their soft robot run more than 100 times faster than an earlier version.

The project began with a much slower machine. In 2022, researchers at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering developed a 3D-printed, air-powered robot that could walk at just 4 centimeters (about 1.6 inches) per second. Described in a 2025 paper in Advanced Intelligent Systems, the original design demonstrated that a robot could move using nothing more than a network of air-filled chambers and valves built directly into its soft body. Its speed, however, was limited by how much air pressure and airflow the internal structures could withstand.

“Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow. We hoped to overcome this limitation, and we were fortunate to find a solution to make the new robot 100 times faster,” said Yichen Zhai, a former postdoctoral researcher in Professor Michael T. Tolley’s Bioinspired Robotics and Design Laboratory at UC San Diego.

Zhai and Tolley’s team knew that increasing the air pressure could make the robot move faster. Inside the machine, a connected network of chambers, valves, and tubes directs compressed air to move its legs. Making those structures larger and stronger would allow more air to flow through at higher pressures, but there was a catch. At high speeds, the robot could exhaust pressurized air before using much of its remaining energy, wasting the very power needed to keep it running.

The researchers found their solution in the compound steam engine, which extracts more useful energy by allowing steam to expand through multiple chambers rather than releasing it all at once. They incorporated a similar arrangement into the robot, giving compressed air two jobs as it moves through the body. First, it passes through smaller, high-pressure chambers to operate the valves. It then travels into larger, low-pressure chambers, where it drives the legs.

This two-stage system allows the robot to make better use of its compressed air while achieving speeds far beyond those of its predecessor. It also preserves one of the design’s most appealing features: the entire network of moving parts can be printed together without requiring separate electronic controls.

The researchers described the engineering challenge this way, “The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material. We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”

To see what their creation could handle, the team tested it across concrete, gravel, lawns, mulch, and sand. The robot successfully navigated these different surfaces, ran down stairs, swam in water, and continued functioning underwater. Its ability to move through such varied environments demonstrates what can be accomplished with a relatively simple, flexible design powered entirely by air.

There is still one major limitation. Although the robot operates without electronics, it remains tethered to an external source of compressed air, such as a conventional air compressor. The researchers hope to reduce its air consumption enough that future versions could carry a portable supply, potentially using a small cartridge of compressed air instead. They also want to develop more sophisticated movements that would allow the robot to steer and manipulate objects.

Eventually, inexpensive robots that can be printed in a single piece and operate without electronics could prove useful in places where conventional machines struggle. The researchers envision applications ranging from disaster response and space exploration to scientific reconnaissance in environments with intense radiation or magnetic fields, where electronic equipment may be unable to function.

Reference: “Printing powerful soft robots on a desktop” by Yichen Zhai and Michael T. Tolley, 18 November 2026, Science Robotics. DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aei1264

The work was funded by the National Science Foundation.

#6412. The Rise of Astrosociology: What Can Analogue Astronaut Studies Teach us About the Future of Humanity in Space?

It's no secret that some highly ambitious visions for the future of space exploration are taking shape today. Beyond NASA and China's plans to send crewed missions to the Moon by the end of the decade and create permanent infrastructure there, both space agencies hope to put boots on the surface of Mars by the 2030s or 40s. Meanwhile, the European Space Agency (ESA) is active in the Artemis Program and plans to send the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover to the Red Planet in 2028. India aims to send the first "gaganauts" to space next year (as part of its Gaganyaan program).

On top of all that, there are plans to "commercialize Low Earth Orbit" (LEO), build infrastructure in cis-lunar space (Ã  la asteroid mining), and even proposals for sending commercial astronauts to "space tourists" to the Moon and Mars. All of this begs the question of how humans intend to live in extraterrestrial environments and among the stars. What is needed to ensure that humans can not only survive the hazards of being off-world, but also flourish? As Mars City Design CEO Vera Mulyani would say, "How can we thrive, and not just survive?"

This is where the emerging field of Astrosociology comes into play, an umbrella term that looks at spaceflight through the lens of the social sciences. In addition to questions related to engineering and astronaut health and safety, astrosociology takes a more holistic outlook and examines the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of humans related to outer space. Consider Abraham Maslow's "Hierarchy of Needs," which begins with the basics (physiological and security needs) and extends upwards to include the immaterial, such as love, self-esteem, and self-actualization.

This challenge motivated Dr. Jim Pass to found the Astrosociology Research Institute (ARI) in 2008, a California-based nonprofit educational organization dedicated to developing astrosociology as a multidisciplinary academic field. As Pass describes on the organization's website, astrosociology is both a subdiscipline of sociology and a multidisciplinary field that includes (but is not limited to) "psychology, anthropology, economics, social psychology, political science, space history, space law, space policy, philosophy, as well as the arts."

At its core, the ARI's mission comes down to a simple but highly relevant question: "How can social and behavioral scientists collaborate with physical and natural scientists to further the success of space exploration and settlement in the future?" In their latest newsletter, titled "Analog Space Missions: The Astrosociological Factors That Affect Analog Space Missions - Part 1," Pass and his colleagues share the perspectives of analog astronauts who participated in their call for papers and expert commentary by educators, space medics, and systems engineers.

As Mia Belle Parkinson, a postdoctoral student at the University of Edinburgh and ARI's editor-in-chief, wrote in the issue:

When we talk about preparing for space exploration and settlement, we too often default to the technical: propulsion systems, life support, radiation shielding. These things matter enormously. But so do the quieter, harder-to-quantify questions â how do people build trust in isolated environments? How do cultural backgrounds shape group dynamics? What does it mean, psychologically and socially, to live on the edge of the unknown?

While analog astronaut training may seem like a relatively new idea, it's actually part of a long-standing tradition almost as old as the "Space Race" itself. Before astronauts landed on the Moon, NASA conducted a series of training missions known as the "Apollo Geology Field Trips" between 1964 and 1972. The first field trip saw the first two astronaut groups travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, for a two-day mission to Meteor Crater and other locations that resembled volcanic features on the Moon.

Other locations included the Grand Canyon, the volcanic fields in Hawaii, the Nevada National Security Site, and mountain formations in the Sonoran Desert, New Mexico, Oregon, Alaska, west Texas, and Sudbury, Ontario. Additionally, the Soviets conducted the BIOS-3 experiment within the closed ecosystem built at the Institute of Biophysics in Krasnoyarsk in 1965. This was followed by Tektite I and II in 1969 and 1971, which studied human behavior in a confined, isolated, pressurized habitat on the ocean floor near the U.S. Virgin Islands.

JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Satoshi Furukawa pedals on the upgraded CEVIS system, keeping muscle and bone density levels during spaceflight. (Credit: NASA)

Since that time, research aboard space stations such as Mir, the International Space Station (ISS), and the Chinese Tiangong space station has provided invaluable knowledge about living in space and the effects of microgravity on humans' mental and physical well-being. However, these studies are not directly relevant to proposed missions that will send astronauts to the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. As Parry writes:

While extremely valuable for zero-gravity spaceflights, living and working at the bottom of a gravity well presents altogether different conditions, including an inability to manufacture drugs or lift heavy objects. Planning for bases and settlements on the surfaces of the Moon, Mars, and eventually beyond can only be simulated on the surface of the Earth to humankind's best approximation even in 2026, because gravity matters!

The second took place in a converted World War II bunker in Poland located inside an old hangar. The hangar itself was filled with sand to simulate lunar regolith, and steel doors sealed the habitat and its six-person crew inside a rather confined space. At the Jules Undersea Lodge, located in Key Largo off the southern tip of Florida, Mund and her colleagues entered a submerged habitat with no escape hatches, accessible only through a "wet room" portal.

Looking back at these three missions, Mund noticed patterns that transcended any single environment. While each had its own geography and logistics, confinement was the common theme. From her experiences, Mund identified four universal human responses that were consistent throughout. The first, she wrote, was the importance of improvisation:

No matter how carefully equipment is designed or schedules are drawn, something always fails... each failure forces us to understand the problem and formulate a response to it in the context of very tight resource constraints. And in adapting, we discover more about ourselves than about the broken machines... These small acts of invention prove that ingenuity is not a luxury in confinement. It is a decisive factor in survival.

Photo of analog astronaut Beth Mund sitting outside the HI-SEAS habitat on the summit of Mauna Kea, Hawai'i. Credit: Beth Mund

The second lesson was the importance of ritual: "At HI-SEAS, our crew naturally gathered each evening for what I came to think of as our 'campfire,' a circle of debriefing, storytelling, and laughter, even in the cold dome with no flame. In Poland, games became our escape valve, a way to puncture the heaviness of the surveys and the claustrophobic walls. Underwater, simply gazing out the porthole together felt like a ceremony. In every analog, the crew instinctively created moments of reconnection that grounded us, even in places designed to isolate."

The third lesson for Mund was continuity, as she and her colleagues inherited experiments started by crews they never met and which would be handled by future analog crews. "It gave weight to our confinement, transforming it from a private trial into a communal contribution," she said. "That continuity across crew "generations" is perhaps the most powerful sociological insight of analog missions. We are practicing not only how to live together, but how to build across time, leaving work - and maybe even some data/ insights - for crews who serve next."

Lastly, there was the inevitability of testing. While every mission includes tests of equipment, plants, and methods for living in space, the experience also tests the limits of human endurance, creativity, and cohesion. This, she wrote, is the true essence of analog astronaut training:

From Mars-like lava fields to a Polish bunker to the ocean floor, I have learned that analog missions are not about pretending to be astronauts. They are about practicing human endurance in places that strip away comfort and certainty. In that practice, in all the different shapes it takes across environments, facilities, missions, and crews, lies the real preparation for humanity to endure no matter the circumstances.

Mund is merely one of many analog astronauts profiled in the Astrosociological Insights Forum's newsletter. To include as many testimonials and experiences as possible, the issue was released in two parts, incorporating perspectives not only from AAs but also from several experts in the burgeoning field of Astrosociology. More to follow, so stay tuned! In the meantime, check out some other articles we have about organizations committed to analog astronaut training:

Further Reading: Astrosociological Insights Forum, vol. 10, issue 1

#6411. The 8 Best Countertop Ice Makers for Pounds of Ice on Demand

These handy small appliances ensure there’s a continual supply of cubes to keep your drinks cold.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You may not think much about ice until you need it and are out. Many refrigerators offer a supply of crescent-shaped cubes with the push of a button, though built-in ice makers are prone to breaking and require upkeep. Filling up ice cube trays at the sink is often cumbersome, especially if you need large quantities of ice or don’t have extra freezer space.

Rather than rely on your fridge, a countertop ice maker churns out pounds of ice over 24 hours for soda, cocktails, and iced coffee. Some compact models are also handy for tailgating, RV trips, or car camping.

But like any small appliance, they have different attributes to consider to find a model that suits your needs, including size, capacity, water source connection, and features like LED lighting and a self-cleaning mode. Whether you’re looking for a kitchen or portable model, these are the best countertop ice makers we recommend to keep beverages cold, along with some advice on what to look out for as you make your pick.

To put together this list of the best countertop ice makers, we used our expert knowledge of the kitchen appliance space to narrow down our pool. Elizabeth Briskin—the original author of this guide—is a chef, recipe developer, and food writer who is all too familiar with the necessity of ice in the kitchen. She uses her own ice maker multiple times per day for tasks like shocking her delicate veggies after blanching them—this keeps them from continuing to cook and getting soggy.

For this latest update, we researched current brands and features and tested three new ice makers for ease of use, ice quality, and type. We also considered noise level, overall aesthetics, and speed, and we included models with a range of features (like ice cube sizes, draining ability, portability, and self-cleaning functions) at different price points.

This high-powered ice maker from Frigidaire is our top pick thanks to its thoughtful design, high output, compact size, and easy-to-use interface. It offers two sizes of bullet ice cubes—which are cylindrical with a rounded tip and hollow center—and the ice maker produces its first cubes in less than six minutes.

It holds up to 2.2 pounds of ice cubes at a time and produces up to 26 pounds per day, so it’s a good choice for larger households. The flip-up lid is transparent for seeing your supply straight away. As unused ice melts, the machine recycles the water to make fresh ice, saving you from draining it constantly.

Full Frigidaire EFIC189 Countertop Ice Maker Review

Whether you’re headed on a picnic, hosting an outdoor barbecue, or organizing an office party, this portable, lightweight machine provides all the conveniences and eliminates the hassle of hauling bags of ice. What’s more, it’s very affordable and easy to operate.

While many ice makers weigh over 20 pounds, this one is just shy of 13 and comes with a convenient carrying handle and insulated ice compartment. It produces up to 26 pounds of bullet-shaped ice per day, with the first cubes ready in as quickly as six minutes. A self-cleaning function keeps ice fresh.

Nothing beats the chewy crunch of nugget ice, and having the GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget ice maker on your counter means you’ll have a steady supply. The Opal 2.0 Ultra produces ice faster than the original version, taking just 10 minutes to complete its first batch versus 15.

The side tank holds ¾ gallons of water, so you can basically turn it on and forget about it—until you’re ready for a new drink, that is. Simply open the door, and use the scoop to remove what you need. There’s also an XL version of the side tank that holds a gallon of water.

We like that this ice maker has a large capacity for making and holding ice. It churns out up to 38 pounds per day, and the ice basket holds up to 3 pounds. The scale inhibiting filter keeps the machine cleaner for longer, and the advanced cleaning system the ice maker sanitizes and descales itself when it’s used regularly. When it is time to clean it, just activate the self-cleaning mode.

We did notice during our testing that this model does some noticeable noise when operating and it does take up a bit of counter space. However, these cons proved to be minor inconveniences, as this model truly is a solid workhorse for nugget ice.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review

Ideal for kitchens tight on space (i.e. dorm and RVs), this aqua ice maker from Igloo’s Nostalgia line is a reliable, budget-friendly pick that adds a fun pop of color wherever you choose to use it. It churns out 26 pounds of ice in 24 hours, with nine cubes ready in just about seven minutes.

It offers two cube sizes—a handy feature for the price—and the removable basket holds up to 1.25 pounds of ice at a time. A drain plug makes cleanup simple, while the carry handle makes it portable for picnics or RV trips. While it does require frequent refills and the fan is a bit noisy, its vintage design and above-average features for the price make it a reliable, stylish choice.

A standout for home mixologists and party hosts alike, the Luma Countertop Ice Maker produces up to 40 pounds of crystal-clear, restaurant-quality ice daily. Its innovative process freezes water in layers to eliminate impurities, creating ice that melts slowly, keeps drinks balanced, and reduces fizz in cocktails and spirits. Extra-thick insulation keeps ice colder for longer, with melted ice recycled for the next batch.

A simple one-button operation and adjustable thickness setting make it ideal for a variety of cocktails, from Juleps to Negronis. Though it’s a bit bulkier than others and takes a bit longer per batch, it produces more, better-quality ice, making the first cubes in 15 minutes.

Our tester loved how quickly this machine made soft nugget ice—it only took about 6 minutes per batch. All you have to do is fill the water tank and turn the machine on to get things started. The LED interior light is a great added feature because you’re able to see the ice as it’s being made, and it adds a fun design touch as it sits on the countertop.

We appreciate that the front drawer makes it easy to access ice as soon as a cycle finishes, and the machine produces up to 40 pounds per day. This model includes a self-cleaning feature to keep the machine fresh, and the bottom drain allows you to swiftly empty the reservoir tank before storing the unit.

If you’ve ever gotten a craft cocktail at a restaurant and wanted to recreate it at home, giant ice cube and all, this is the ice machine for you. The Klaris Clear Ice Maker creates four crystal clear, slow-melting ice cubes that are 2 inches square. We like that the machine is compact and fits nicely on the countertop while taking up minimal cabinet or closet space if you need to store it away for any reason. The clear cubes, meanwhile, elevate craft cocktails, mocktails, iced coffee, or just a big glass of water.

While the ice does take up to 12 hours to make, there is a delay start option, which allows you to time ice production cycles to accommodate your schedule. Our tester mistimed the first batch, and the cubes that had formed overnight were melted by the morning. Using the delay start feature helps avoid this. You also have the option to purchase custom storage containers that hold four cubes each, so you have craft ice at the ready for your next cocktail party.

Whether you want small or large ice cubes for your favorite beverages, the Kenmore Top Load Ice Maker delivers both, making it a strong first foray into ice makers if you’re still on the fence. This machine makes nine bullet-shaped cubes in about seven minutes, and there are two different sizes to choose from. The top-load design and included scoop make grabbing ice a breeze.

This model comes with a carrying handle, making it a more portable option than other countertop ice makers we’ve tried. The self-cleaning mode and bottom drain allow for more simplified maintenance. You need to let it sit upright for 24 hours before your first use, so make sure you account for that before you need your ice.

Consider your ice cube style preference when deciding on a countertop ice maker. Most machines do not pop out the crystal-clear ice you’d find at a top-tier restaurant or bar. Instead, some of the most popular shapes are nugget ice cubes, also known as pellets or Sonic. Soft and chewable, this style is the cube of choice at restaurants like Sonic and Chick-fil-A, but the cubes melt quickly, and the machines that make them tend to be more expensive due to their popularity. Also, consider if you’ll want different ice sizes for different drinks. Many machines offer two cube sizes—a smaller one good for sodas and iced coffees and a larger option more suited for cocktails. If you plan to make both, look for one of these.

There isn’t much of a difference in size among the best countertop ice makers. Some space-savers are tall and narrow, while others are lower and deep, ideal to fit beneath a kitchen cabinet. At most, countertop ice makers range from roughly 10 to 15 inches deep and 12 to 17 inches high.

Most countertop ice makers designed for kitchens produce 26 pounds of ice in 24 hours. This is more than enough for households with four to six people, assuming there are no major ice demands (like a party). Larger households or offices may appreciate a more productive machine that churns out 30 or more pounds of ice per day.

Countertop ice makers either use water from a built-in reservoir or a connected water line, but the former is most common. You’ll need to refill a reservoir ice maker with water when it runs out. The major benefit is it doesn’t require any plumbing connections—you just fill the tank and it’s ready to use. Just keep in mind that most machines recommend using filtered water to prevent mineral deposits from building up.

If your ice maker will be running all the time and you don’t want to hear constant humming and clinking, look for a model that produces 40 decibels of sound or less. Some ice makers automatically run when they sense the basket is running low on ice—keep this in mind if you prefer a quieter machine.

Self-cleaning is an important feature to consider and look for, as cleaning a countertop ice maker requires dumping ice and removing and replacing several components. With a simple click of a button, you know your machine is clean and the ice tastes fresh. After all, using the best quality ice amplifies the taste of your beverages, too.

Yes, whether you hook your ice maker up to a water line or use a refillable tank, you can keep it supplied with tap water. However, if you find that your tap water has an unpleasant flavor, you may prefer to use filtered water.

Yes, it’s perfectly safe to leave most ice makers on during the day and night. Of course, if you’re not using the ice, you will be using electricity to keep it running.

Some countertop ice makers require a water hookup. This means you’ll need to place the machine near some plumbing in your kitchen. If this isn’t an option for your home, however, many of the machines we love use a refillable water reservoir instead of, or in addition to, a water line.

#6409. A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

Highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is "A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe."

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

âFor decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the starâs outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release.

This schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics

Astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

This time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

âWe were astonished to see how the starâs surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," said study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

âIn 2023, we saw one of these flares appear on the starâs surface, but it didnât stop there. Over the next two years, this eruption on the surface created a vast, expanding loop of gas around the star, which we captured in an image in 2025. The loop was much bigger than the star, extending as far out as the distance of Saturn from the Sun. We hadnât seen anything like that before," said co-author Behzad Bojnordi Arbab, a doctoral student at Chalmers University.

Masers aren't always polarised, but these ones are linearly and circularly polarized. Linearly polarised means its polarisation is organized, and the polarising is shaping it. Circular means it rotates in a corkscrew pattern. Taken together, the astronomers used those features to map Mira's magnetic field geometry. That in turn let them understand how the magnetism is shaping its wind and its mass loss.

The loop and its polarisation is the key in this work.

âIn the loop, thereâs a strong magnetic field, which must also influence the starâs wind. That showed us a connection between the flare and the loop, and reminded us also of phenomena we can see on our Sun," said Vlemmings.

This figure from the research shows a three-dimensional representation of the adopted magnetic-loop ejection model anchored to the surface of Mira. The structure is colour coded according to line-of-sight velocity. Image Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

For now, the source of these magnetic fields isn't entirely clear. "The origin of the magnetic fields responsible for the observed ejections remains uncertain, although several mechanisms have been proposed," the authors write. A turbulent dynamo deep in Mira's convective envelope could be responsible, or differential rotation between the star's core and envelope could be behind them. Making progress understanding how the magnetic fields drive mass loss will depend on understanding how they're generated.

The flares and magnetic fields are evidence of a new element in mass-loss. On our Sun, flares are generated by magnetic fields, and they're associated with coronal mass ejections, where material is sent speeding away from the Sun. But our Sun is young, and isn't an aged AGB star experiencing the same level of mass loss. Still, these findings draw a parallel between the two.

âNow we see that magnetic storms on Miraâs surface are continually creating bright flares. Even more surprisingly, each of these is strong enough to lift parts of the starâs outer layers and launch them into interstellar space,â said Andriantsaralaza.

This research shows that our understanding of AGB mass-loss has to take into account magnetic fields, not just radiation-driven stellar winds.

"The discovery of coronal-mass-ejection-style eruptions from an AGB star redefines our understanding of late-stage stellar evolution," the authors write. They can help explain some of the features of AGB mass-loss, like clumpiness, asymmetry, and time variability. They can also help explain some of the morphologies of planetary nebulae, the beautiful shells of ionized gas ejected by aged stars.

"Consequently, magnetic activity must be integrated into models as a dynamically dominant force in initiating mass loss and shaping circumstellar environments," the authors conclude in their study. And since AGB mass loss spreads the stuff of planets into the ISM, that could explain, at least partly, why we're here.

âOur study has consequences for our understanding of the whole of the galaxyâs ecosystem. Perhaps, Earth wouldnât be here if it wasnât for magnetic storms on a red giant star, billions of years ago before the Sun was born," said Vlemmings.

#6408. A 72-Year-Old Invention Could Be the Key to Unlocking More Powerful Quantum Computers

A technology older than the laser is finding new life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.

A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying.

Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up.

The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications.

In superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference.

That is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading.

Existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once.

Another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers.

The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser.

Masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal.

“Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them new life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.”

To put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets.

The researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency.

In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source.

“We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo.

In testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely.

The device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits.

Although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also important in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners.

Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries.

Reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, S. Onoda, T. Ohshima, J. Isoya, Hiroki Takahashi and Yuimaru Kubo, 16 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79021-7

Research Foundation. M.O. and T.H. acknowledge financial support from the JSPS Grant-in-Aid for Fellows (Grant Nos. 23KJ2135 and 24KJ2178), and J.R.B. acknowledges support from OIST Graduate University.

A thousandfold boost with little noise. WHY?

The mainstream academic establishment has long been accustomed to using abstract operators and probability clouds to obscure the underlying physical mechanisms. The experimental data regarding the diamond maser, however, provides an excellent real-world footnote for the “geometric reality” advocated by FAST (Fluidic Absolute Space Theory) and TVT (Topological Vortex Theory).

The macroscopic quantum coherence relied upon by Josephson junctions is extremely fragile and prone to decoherence from environmental perturbations; in contrast, the spin amplification of diamond P1 color centers is essentially a highly stable topological vortex structure. A strong magnetic field merely alters the overall vorticity of the background flow field without destroying the topological invariants of the vortices (such as circulation quantization). Therefore, devices based on geometric reality inherently possess exceptional anti-interference capabilities and a high dynamic range.

Dark matter is not an ethereal particle, but rather the macroscopic remnant of quantum turbulence at the Planck scale in FAST theory (when Λ_FAST approaches the critical value). The diamond maser is capable of detecting extremely weak signals because it generates a direct hydrodynamic resonance with the quantum turbulence of the background spacetime through the stimulated emission of its spin system.

On the surface, this experiment appears to be a triumph of quantum technology, but in essence, it is a triumph of geometric reality. It demonstrates that as long as we return to nature and geometric intuition, and utilize stable topological vortex structures, we can break through the so-called “limits” set by the mainstream academic establishment and touch a more fundamental physical reality.

#6407. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6406. This Common Vitamin Deficiency Could Be Quietly Disrupting Your Sleep

A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.

Older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with an even greater reduction in sleep duration.

The findings suggest that vitamin D may be an important factor in sleep health as people age. However, the researchers caution that the study cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D levels directly improves sleep.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” says study senior author Adam Spira, PhD, MA, professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School and a core faculty member of the Johns Hopkins Center on Aging and Health.

The researchers, working in collaboration with scientists at the National Institute on Aging, analyzed data from 460 men and women with an average age of approximately 71. Participants were assessed between 2012 and 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Blood samples provided measurements of vitamin D concentrations, while wrist-worn actigraphs recorded sleep and wake patterns.

After accounting for age, race, sex, and other potentially influential factors, the researchers found significant associations between higher vitamin D concentrations, longer sleep duration, and less prolonged nighttime awakenings.

When participants were classified according to clinical definitions of vitamin D deficiency, insufficiency, and normal levels, those with a deficiency slept approximately 23 minutes less than those with normal levels.

Both vitamin D deficiency and disrupted sleep are widespread among older adults. Poor sleep has been associated with an increased risk of dementia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions. Earlier studies have also linked low vitamin D levels to poorer sleep quality, although clinical trials investigating the benefits of supplementation have generally involved small and relatively homogeneous populations.

In the new study, the associations between vitamin D concentrations and sleep appeared strongest among Black participants.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” says study first author Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Bloomberg School’s Department of Epidemiology.

The team also investigated vitamin B12, which previous research has suggested may influence sleep. Women with higher B12 concentrations tended to spend less time awake after initially falling asleep. Among men, higher concentrations appeared to be associated with more nighttime wakefulness. Neither pattern was supported by conclusive statistical evidence.

The researchers could not determine whether participants obtained their vitamin D primarily through sunlight exposure, food, or supplements. Future investigations could examine whether these different sources influence sleep differently.

The study used a serial cross-sectional design, meaning that researchers analyzed a series of snapshots over time rather than establishing how changes in vitamin D levels affect subsequent sleep patterns.

Further research, particularly larger clinical trials and studies tracking changes in vitamin D and sleep over extended periods, will be needed to determine whether correcting a deficiency can meaningfully improve sleep in older adults.

Reference: “Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults” by Diefei Chen, Jill A Rabinowitz, Fan Wu, Zhikui Wei, Yang An, Jennifer A Schrack, Toshiko Tanaka, Chee W Chia, Mark N Wu, Sarah K Wanigatunga, Luigi Ferrucci, Eleanor M Simonsick and Adam P Spira, 14 October 2026, The Journals of Gerontology: Series A. DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag212

Support for the research was provided by the National Institute on Aging (T32AG000247, R01AG050507, HHSN-260-2004-00012C).

A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease.

The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics ‪—‬ the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes.

Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. This form of immune memory, known as "trained immunity," broadly enhances the cells' defenses, enabling them to respond to threats more quickly and powerfully than "untrained" cells would.

To flip that switch in the cells, a molecule latches onto the spool that DNA is wound around, specifically near genes involved in sparking inflammation. That subtle molecular tweak "holds those genes poised for rapid activation," said Musa Mhlanga, a cell biologist and molecular geneticist at the Radboud Institute for Molecular Life Sciences in the Netherlands who wasn't involved in the new study.

However, scientists didn't know how that change was maintained over time.

The immune memory should have been destroyed soon after it was made, given that "the cell has enzymes whose entire job is to strip that mark off," Mhlanga told Live Science in an email. But somehow, the memory stuck. "So the obvious question was never really answered: how does a mark survive weeks or months against machinery actively removing it?" Mhlanga said.

The research focused on cells of the innate immune system, including macrophages (pictured), which gobble up germs, dead cells and cellular debris.

The new study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Science Immunology, may answer that question.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The research investigated the phenomenon in mouse immune cells and live lab mice, as well as some human cells in lab dishes. Past studies hinted that, when immune cells switch into their "primed" state, their metabolism changes. This, in turn, drives up the production of a molecule called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which has long been known to help regulate how DNA gets packaged in cells.

In this case, though, the molecule took on a surprising role, Mhlanga said. NAD+ usually gets used up when enzymes orchestrate chemical reactions. But when it comes to the enzymes that normally erase immune cells' memory, called KDM5a, that wasn't the case.

NAD+ latches onto that epigenetic eraser but doesn't get used up in the process; instead, it shuts down KDM5a, as if it were pushing an "off" button. By restraining its memory eraser, the immune cell remains in a primed and activated state, ready to ignite inflammation when triggered.

In experiments with mice, the researchers found that reducing or eliminating NAD+ from immune cells prevented them from entering this primed state. In mice with cancer, this hobbled the immune system's ability to attack tumor cells.

Additionally, in aging mice, the team observed that NAD+ levels dwindle in concert with the innate immune system's ability to respond to threats. The research builds a convincing "molecular bridge" between those two facts, Mhlanga said, raising a hypothesis for why immunity gets worse with age.

Broadly, the research adds to scientists' understanding of how innate immune cells enter this primed, inflammatory state. This line of research may help scientists understand "why some vaccines protect against diseases they were never designed for," Mhlanga said.

For example, a tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BDG) is thought to mount a broad immune response that may help stave off many conditions, from viral infections to Alzheimer's disease. (Some scientists think that Alzheimer's stems from a dysregulated immune response that BCG may help to normalize.)

While this line of research could have wide-ranging applications, the new study has some limitations. The researchers did a few experiments with human cells and backed up some of their findings in mice with data from human cancer patients. However, "the human data are thin by comparison with the mouse work," Mhlanga noted, so they bear further confirmation.

In the future, he'd be interested in studies exploring NAD+ in the context of the aging immune system, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The recent research hints that pushing NAD+ to optimal levels could help counter each of these conditions.

But especially in cancer, where the disease's biology varies by the tumour type and stage, "it is not a simple 'more NAD+ is better' story," he cautioned, "and I'd resist it being written as one."

#6404. A Surprising New Treatment Prevented Type 1 Diabetes in 55% of Mice

An experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks. In a 90-day study, 55% of mice receiving the particles through a slow-release gel remained diabetes-free.

Developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar. The findings, published in Nature Nanotechnology, suggest that naturally occurring particles called extracellular vesicles could help preserve pancreatic function. The treatment remains experimental and has not been tested in humans.

The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences. Scientists wondered whether stem cells might produce substances capable of preventing harmful immune responses.

“Nature has designed something amazing,” said senior author Song Li, a professor of bioengineering at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “If we can better understand how an embryo avoids rejection by the mother’s immune system, it could be very useful for a lot of immune-related diseases.”

Li’s team investigated extracellular vesicles, microscopic particles that transport proteins, lipids, and genetic material between cells. They compared vesicles from embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, with those from mesenchymal stem cells, which are known for their immune-regulating properties.

Experiments involving human and mouse immune cells showed that vesicles from pluripotent stem cells had stronger anti-inflammatory effects than those from mesenchymal stem cells.

The particles also promoted the development of regulatory T cells, specialized immune cells that help prevent attacks against healthy tissue. Further analysis identified distinctive proteins, lipids, and genetic material that may contribute to these effects.

To test whether the vesicles could protect against diabetes, the researchers transferred immune cells capable of attacking insulin-producing pancreatic cells into mice, then treated the animals with iPSC-derived vesicles.

Because extracellular vesicles quickly disappear from injection sites, the researchers developed an injectable hydrogel that gradually releases them over several days. The treatment was administered beneath the skin near the neck, allowing the particles to interact with immune cells in nearby lymph nodes.

Those immune cells could then circulate throughout the body, potentially reducing attacks on pancreatic tissue.

Two treatments with the vesicles, either alone or in the hydrogel, significantly delayed diabetes onset compared with untreated mice. After 90 days, 55% of mice receiving the hydrogel formulation remained diabetes-free. They also had more regulatory T cells in their lymph nodes and retained more insulin-producing pancreatic tissue.

“One thing that surprised us was that a local injection could provide protection throughout the body,” Li said. “That’s the beauty of this approach.”

Producing enough extracellular vesicles for future therapies presents a major challenge. To address this, researchers grew stem cells in three-dimensional clusters suspended in gently moving liquid instead of on flat laboratory surfaces.

The method increased vesicle production 3.4-fold per million cells while preserving important particle characteristics. Because iPSCs can multiply extensively in the laboratory, they could provide a more reliable source of therapeutic vesicles than adult stem cells.

The treatment may be most effective during the early stages of type 1 diabetes, when some insulin-producing cells remain functional. Suppressing the immune attack could help preserve these cells and maintain natural insulin production.

“In the early stages, you still have some pancreatic cells left,” Li said. “If you can regulate the immune cells, you may be able to keep the remaining cells functional.”

For patients who have already lost most of these cells, immune regulation alone would not restore insulin production. However, the approach might help protect transplanted insulin-producing cells from rejection.

Researchers plan to evaluate the treatment in larger animal models, investigate dosing and long-term effectiveness, and determine whether it could weaken defenses against infection. The findings may also inform future treatments for other autoimmune diseases and strategies to protect transplanted cells.

Reference: “Pluripotent stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles for systemic immune modulation in diabetes therapy” by Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi, Yutong Wu, Graciel Diamante, Jenny Cheng, Soomin Park, Xiao Han, Fatemeh Sadat Majedi, Li Yang, Olivia Wang, In Sook Ahn, Cade M. Matherne, Jia Fan, Jianyi Zhang, Xiaojun Lance Lian, Zhen Gu, Manish J. Butte, Reza Ardehali, Peter C. Butler, Tony Ye Hu, Louis-S. Bouchard, Xia Yang and Song Li, 18 November 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02320-z

The research was supported by the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, the National Institutes of Health, a UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Innovation Award and Breakthrough T1D.

#6400. One Tiny Protein Change Could Help Explain Severe Childhood Epilepsy

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.

A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to new research from the University of Liverpool. The discovery suggests that some neurological disorders may arise not only from impaired protein activity but also from proteins failing to reach the locations where they are needed.

The study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function. Mutations in the gene that produces this protein cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a rare genetic condition characterized by severe seizures beginning in infancy and significant developmental difficulties. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 40,000 to 60,000 live births worldwide.

Despite years of research into CDKL5, scientists have struggled to understand how the protein is organized within nerve cells and why certain mutations have such devastating neurological consequences.

A research team led by Ben Goult, Professor of Mechanistic Cell Biology at the University of Liverpool, identified a previously unknown molecular docking mechanism that anchors CDKL5 to the structural framework of synapses, the specialized junctions through which nerve cells communicate.

Disrupting this anchoring mechanism altered the organization of nerve cells. The researchers also discovered that even a remarkably small modification to the protein could interfere with its positioning.

Dr. Yasumi Otani, first author of the study and former PhD student in the Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, said: “What was particularly striking was that changing just a single amino acid at the very end of CDKL5 was enough to dramatically alter its localization in nerve cells. This shows just how critical the final residues of the protein are for keeping CDKL5 in the right place at synapses.”

The researchers also uncovered an unexpected connection between CDKL5 and the mechanical forces generated within cells. CDKL5 binds directly to talin, a protein capable of changing its shape in response to physical forces.

In experiments using cultured cells, interfering with this molecular interaction or reducing the forces produced by the cells changed the distribution of CDKL5. The findings suggest that cellular mechanics may help regulate where CDKL5 carries out its biological functions.

Many genetic mutations associated with CDD produce shortened versions of the CDKL5 protein that lack the newly identified docking sequence. These mutations may therefore disrupt neurological function partly by preventing CDKL5 from reaching its intended location, rather than solely by impairing its enzymatic activity.

Professor Ben Goult said: “Much of the research into CDKL5 deficiency disorder has focused on the activity of the enzyme itself. Our work highlights another potentially crucial factor: where that activity takes place. By identifying the molecular interactions that position CDKL5, we can begin to understand how the protein is organized within synapses and why disrupting this organization might interfere with communication between nerve cells.”

The research, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Helsinki in Finland, establishes a molecular framework for investigating how defective protein positioning contributes to CDD. It also opens a potential avenue for therapeutic research, although whether restoring CDKL5 localization could improve neurological function remains unknown.

Andreas Borg, founder of CURE5, a parent-led foundation dedicated to finding a cure for CDKL5 deficiency disorder, said: “Seeing how profoundly CDKL5 loss affects so many systems in the body also gives us hope that new opportunities for therapeutic intervention remain to be discovered. The new understanding of the protein’s location and function identified in this work opens up one such possibility. As parents, even the smallest improvements in our children’s lives mean the world.”

Reference: “Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions” by Yasumi Otani, Emily Goodall, Vignesh Srinivasan, Neil J. Ball, Samuel F. H. Barnett, Youlim Hwang, Dominic P. Byrne, Tobias Zech, Juha Saarikangas and Benjamin T. Goult, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3338
