#6345. The Sky Today on Monday, November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard

A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6344. Sitting behind the wheel may do something unusual to your heart rate

Driving keeps the heart above its resting rate for longer, even when the body remains seated and inactive.

Sitting behind the wheel is usually treated as no different from sitting anywhere else. Heart-rate readings that were collected for a week from 57 young adults in Texas now suggest otherwise.

During the time these people spent driving, their heart rates remained above resting level almost throughout. A return to resting level was recorded about half as often as during other inactive hours.

Their hearts were not found to beat faster in the car than during those other hours. The resting pace was simply reached less often while a person was driving.

The study was designed and supervised by Ioannis Pavlidis who is a computer science professor at the University of Houston.

Colleagues from the same university and from the Texas A&M Transportation Institute worked with him.

Pavlidis said that a driver has to keep watching the road and deciding what to do next.

“The body may be sitting, but the mind is working,” he said. According to him, it is in the heart rate that this mental work can be seen.

What the study isn’t able to show is that driving itself kept anyone’s heart rate up. The comparison that was made was between time spent driving and other inactive time in one week.

There are more differences between these two kinds of time than the car alone.

Posture and caffeine are on the list of them that the authors gave and so are passengers. How urgently a driver needed to arrive is on that list as well.

The group consisted of 30 men and 27 women with an average age of about 26. Most of them were office workers.

A personal iPhone and Apple Watch were used by each participant from Monday through Sunday.

Every car was fitted with a small plug-in device by which each period of driving could be recorded. The watch was the source of the heart rate readings to which weather and traffic conditions were matched.

The rest of each day was labeled with the help of activity data from the phone and the watch. Any recorded minute in which a person was neither driving nor physically active was taken into the comparison.

Such minutes may have been spent at work or at home or somewhere else entirely.

The batteries of the iPhone and Apple Watch had usually run out by early evening. It is for this reason that the recordings cover daytime hours alone.

It was Pavlidis’ group at the Affective and Data Computing Laboratory that averaged the readings minute by minute. The recordings that resulted came to 177,318 minutes which is close to 3,000 hours.

No heart-rate reading existed for 13.6% of the driving minutes or for 3.5% of other inactive minutes. Neither speed nor traffic was found to be linked to the readings that were missing.

Driving took up about a tenth of that time. There were 973 trips in total and half of them were over within 15 minutes. A crash or a traffic ticket was generally not part of these drives.

Before any single minute could be judged, the team had to know each person’s resting heart rate.

An estimate of it is produced by the Apple Watch once a day. These daily estimates were averaged by the team across the whole week.

While a person was driving, their heart rate was above their own resting level 93.7% of the time on average. The figure for other inactive time was 81.3%.

Yet a higher heart rate in the car was not what the Houston team found. During driving, it averaged 11.2 beats per minute above resting level. The average for other inactive time was 11.5 beats above resting level.

A gap as small as that could have come up by chance.

Where driving did differ was in how little the heart rate varied. Its typical spread was 7.98 beats per minute during driving and 12.40 beats during other inactive time.

Heart rates dropped to resting level 2.46 times per hour during other inactive time and 1.31 times per hour while driving.

On weekdays, the two shares of time above resting level were 93.8% and 82.1%.

Weekends showed the same pattern, although people then spend their hours outside the car differently.

According to Pavlidis, a workout also raises heart rate, but the body becomes fitter as a result of it. From the time that is spent behind the wheel, no benefit of that kind is gained.

Yasmine Bouzid and the other authors also examined what a higher or lower heart rate was tied to.

During driving, there were two things that stood out from the rest. Time of day was the first since heart rates were higher in drives after noon than in the morning.

The second was the amount by which the driver’s wrist had turned in the minute before. The gyroscope of the Apple Watch supplied this measure which was treated as a sign of steering.

Away from the car, the list that was found was a broader one. On it were age and sex along with time of day and the Big Five personality trait of openness.

For this, the authors offered one reason which they regarded as possible. Driving is a single task whose demands remain fairly steady from one minute to the next.

Many different situations are covered by the inactive time that is spent away from the car.

Because a drive is repeated day after day, an example using anxiety was worked through by the team.

The volunteers had filled out the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, which scores a tendency to feel anxious from 20 to 80. The lowest score that was found in this group was 20 while the highest was 61.

Over every recorded minute of driving, the team’s heart-rate model was then run twice. A score of 20 was given to every driver in the first of these runs. In the second run, it was a score of 61 that every driver was given.

The heart rate that the model predicted with the score of 61 was higher by 0.99 beats per minute.

What the Houston team then did was to count such beats over a whole year. For a person who drives eight hours a day, the model projected about 173,000 extra heartbeats.

It came to roughly 11,000 extra heartbeats when the same was done for a 30-minute daily drive.

It was only as illustrations that these totals were described by Pavlidis and his coauthors. What they show is how a small difference accumulates, and not what anyone’s risk of heart disease is.

There were only young adults from Texas among the 57 volunteers, and none was followed for more than a week. Older drivers, professional drivers, or people with heart disease may not show the results that were found here.

It will take years of following drivers before the health side of this can be judged. Only then can it be learned whether more time above resting heart rate predicts heart problems.

Pavlidis said that driving is something many people can’t do without. What his lab in Houston wants to find out is how the same trips could be made less demanding.

The Texas A&M Transportation Institute, where study co-author Michael Manser works, is supporting the lab through 2027.

The people who are to be studied next include long-distance commuters and those who drive for a living.

Rideshare drivers are an example of the latter. The groups are meant to be bigger, more varied, and followed for longer.

There is one more question that self-driving cars from Waymo and Tesla have raised for the lab. What does a rider’s heart rate do when it is the vehicle that handles the driving?

The full study was published in the journal npj Digital Public Health.

#6343. A con man claimed his secret gold mine was paying for a $2 million castle in Death Valley, but the mine never existed

A man nicknamed "Death Valley Scotty" said his gold mine paid for Scotty's Castle. That wasn't true. Here's what really happened.

In the 1920s, reporters who made the trip to a remote canyon in northern Death Valley found a Spanish-style mansion rising out of the desert.

Walter Scott, better known as “Death Valley Scotty,” had an explanation for it. He was building the two million dollar home, he said, with profits from his secret gold mine.

There was no mine. The house belonged to Albert Mussey Johnson, a Chicago insurance millionaire who had been sending Scotty money for years, according to the National Park Service.

When reporters asked Johnson about it, he agreed that Scotty owned the place and described himself simply as “Scotty’s banker.”

A century later, the estate still carries the con man’s name. But Scotty’s Castle has been closed to regular visits since a flash flood in October 2015, and in October 2026 the park said the earliest it could fully reopen is November 2028.

Scott was born in Kentucky in 1872. He ran away as a boy to join two of his brothers in Nevada, worked at the Harmony Borax Works and rode in Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West Show, according to the park.

After leaving the show in 1902, he turned to gold prospecting and convinced several wealthy businessmen that he had a claim to a fabulous gold mine in Death Valley.

Scott offered to split the profits if they first put up money to extract the ore. When no gold arrived, most of his investors decided they had been conned and backed out.

In July 1905, Scotty traveled by train to Chicago with a roll of money, falsely claiming to have struck it rich in a Death Valley mine. The trip broke the travel time record and opened doors among the wealthy elite.

According to the park’s biography of Johnson, he had already invested in Scotty’s mine in 1904, and he kept sending money even after the person he sent to check on Scott reported that there was no gold mine.

In 1906, Johnson tried to visit the mine himself. On the way into the valley, his party was attacked in what became known as the Battle of Wingate Pass, and Scotty’s brother Warner was shot. The park describes Scotty as a flamboyant con artist and showman.

When Johnson finally made it to Death Valley, Scotty took him on a grueling trek by horseback, apparently expecting the desert to be too much for him.

Johnson had been badly injured in a train accident in his youth. Instead, he stayed nearly a month, and his health improved dramatically in the dry, sunny climate.

He never saw the mine and was almost certainly being swindled, the park says, but he did not seem to mind. The two men became lifelong friends.

Johnson went on to buy land in spring-fed Grapevine Canyon, about 3,000 feet above sea level, eventually owning 1,500 acres.

His wife, Bessie, suggested building something more comfortable than the canvas tents they had been using, so they could “get away from the rattlesnakes and scorpions.”

Work on what they called Death Valley Ranch began in the 1920s, and the garage built in 1922 served as the workshop for the construction.

Scotty, who recognized a good story, told everyone the house was his. Even the concrete posts along the property’s fence were stamped with an “S” for Scotty and a “J” for Johnson, the true owner.

Construction stopped in 1931, when Johnson discovered that, because of a surveying error, he had been building on federal land.

The Great Depression was beginning to take hold, and the work never resumed. The castle was left incomplete, and its swimming pool was never finished.

Johnson died in 1948 and left most of his fortune and property to the Gospel Foundation, which he had founded two years earlier.

Scotty had the right to live at the castle for the rest of his life. He died in January 1954. Johnson had hoped the National Park Service would one day buy the property, and in 1970 it did.

For decades, rangers in period costume led tours through the house and told the story of the Johnsons and their friend.

On the night of October 18, 2015, Scotty’s Castle received 2 3/4 inches of rain, about a year’s worth, in five hours, after a half-inch the day before.

A flash flood of mud and rocks poured down Grapevine Canyon at an estimated 3,200 cubic feet per second, according to the park. On steep slopes like these, heavy rain can trigger flash floods faster than expected.

Rangers sheltered with about 20 stranded visitors on the rim of Ubehebe Crater that night, and one ranger watched power poles and metal dumpsters float out of the canyon. Nobody was hurt.

The main house mostly escaped the flood. The historic garage, which served as the visitor center, did not. The water broke through its windows, doors and walls and left four feet of mud and rocks inside.

The unfinished pool filled many feet deep with mud and debris, and most of the 8-mile road through the canyon was destroyed.

Repairs were under way in April 2021 when contractors arrived one morning to find the garage on fire, with flames spreading to the neighboring Longshed. The garage was destroyed.

A state investigation found the fire started inside the building but could not determine a cause and found no evidence of arson.

The park has given two figures for how far the garage repairs had gone, 37% in a June 2021 release and 60% on its recovery page. One of the upgrades being installed was fire sprinklers.

In 2019, the park expected to reopen the castle in October 2021. After the fire, the target moved to 2023. It is now November 2028 at the earliest.

The park lists funding and staffing problems, legal reviews to protect historic and natural features, contracting issues, unforeseen conditions, the pandemic, more flooding and the fire.

The repairs cost about $71 million, split into separate projects so they could be funded from different sources.

Some of the work is done. New berms and flood walls finished in January 2023 protected the historic district when the remnants of Hurricane Hilary hit the park that August. The road through the canyon has been rebuilt.

The next phase, expected to start in 2027, covers the parking lot, the Longshed and the historic Gas Tank House, which will become a small visitor contact station in place of the burned garage.

After that, curators will return the furnishings and museum collections to the house before interior tours can resume.

Until then, the only way in is a guided tour. This season, rangers and guides from the Death Valley Natural History Association are leading exterior tours of the grounds on most Saturdays and Sundays through April 17.

Tickets are sold through the association. Bonnie Clare Road, the 8-mile route through Grapevine Canyon, remains closed to the public, including pedestrians.

Once the castle is fully reopened, the park plans to open it each year from late fall through early spring.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s October 2026 announcement on Scotty’s Castle tours, its pages on the Scotty’s Castle flood and recovery, building the castle, Death Valley Scotty, Albert Mussey Johnson and the showmen of Death Valley tourism, and its releases on the 2021 fire, the fire investigation and the repairs four years after the flood.

#6341. Nov. 23, 1221: The birth of Alfonso the Wise

On Nov. 23, 1221, Alfonso X was born in Spain, the son of King Ferdinand III of Castile and Leon. By the time he succeeded his father in 1252, Alfonso was already known as a scholar – though he demonstrated his military might as well, putting down several revolts and annexing Murcia.

Known as Alfonso the Wise, the king pioneered efforts to translate Arabic and Andalusian works of astronomy into the vernacular Castilian. His multicultural court authored scholarly works and engineered scientific instruments, as well as collecting an extensive library of works on astrology and astronomy. Alfonso also commissioned the Alfosine Tables, astronomical tables based on Arabic sources and updated with new observations – facilitated by new astronomical instruments constructed at Alfonso’s orders. The work included stellar and planetary positions and became the standard for astronomy in Europe for the late medieval and early Renaissance periods.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6340. The second most common element in the universe is actually running out here on Earth

Most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious…

Most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious yellow band in the Sun’s light spectrum that did not match any known element.

The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.

Humanity had identified an element in starlight 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away before anyone held a sample of it.

Confirmation took decades. The Scottish chemist William Ramsay finally isolated terrestrial helium in 1895, releasing it from a uranium-bearing mineral nearly 27 years after Lockyer first saw its signature.

That long delay hints at the problem now reshaping hospitals and laboratories. Helium is the second-most-abundant element in the universe, yet it is genuinely rare on Earth.

The contradiction comes down to gravity. Helium is so light that it drifts upward, escapes the atmosphere, and is lost to space forever. Our Moon even collects traces of the gases our planet sheds. The cosmic abundance simply never settled here.

The helium we use does not come from the Big Bang reservoir that fills the cosmos. It forms underground, atom by atom, as radioactive uranium and thorium decay within the crust.

Those elements decay on almost unimaginable timescales. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and thorium-232 closer to 14 billion years, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Each decay releases the alpha particles that become helium.

The same slow chemistry that shaped Earth’s crust over billions of years also governs its helium. No factory can shortcut that process, which is why no large-scale method exists to manufacture the gas artificially.

This is the deeper reason the current squeeze matters. A shortfall in most materials invites more mining or more production. A helium shortfall invites neither, because the planet replenishes its supply only as fast as atoms decay.

Producers extract helium as a trace component of natural gas, and only deposits with high enough concentrations are worth tapping. That narrow geology leaves the market exposed to plant shutdowns and trade disruptions.

The strain is already visible. Hospitals consume roughly a third of the world’s helium to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, and analysts expect global demand to double by 2035 as semiconductor and electric-vehicle manufacturing expand.

The hunt for fresh supply is reaching parts of the world that never produced helium before. In Tanzania, the Southern Rukwa project finalized its mining agreements in May 2026, positioning the country to extract helium at a commercial scale. Qatar has also moved to bring new capacity online.

Policy decisions have added uncertainty. The United States sold its Federal Helium System, once the planet’s largest single source, to the industrial gas company Messer in June 2024, ending nearly a century of public stewardship, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management confirmed.

Newer MRI machines now seal and recirculate their helium, and many labs capture and re-liquefy every drop they can. These measures buy time, much as a simple scan can buy a patient time. Whether they arrive fast enough is the open question.

There is a quiet symmetry to the helium story. We discovered it by looking up at a star, much as a meteorite can reveal a vanished world, and we may yet preserve it by looking down into the rocks that hoard it.

For now, the element that fills birthday balloons remains one of the most strategically important substances on the planet. It reminds us that some of Earth’s rarest things are those we first noticed in the heavens.

The full study was published in the journal Physics Today.

#6339. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Warming has intensified El Niño’s impacts on weather around the globe, making it harder to prepare

Large waves, driven eastward by the strengthening El Niño in the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, battered the city of Oceanside California (shown) on October 9.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento.  And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

#6337. The amazing Crab Nebula

One of my personal favorite objects in the night sky is the Crab Nebula (M1). It’s No. 1 on Charles Messier’s list, although I don’t think he ordered his objects by how cool they are (a missed opportunity!). It’s not exactly impressive visually in most scopes — mostly a gray blob, or a spiky gray blob in larger apertures — but it’s one of those targets that if you know what you are looking at, it becomes immensely more interesting to observe.

The Crab Nebula burst onto the scene in 1054 C.E., when a massive star in the constellation Taurus collapsed in on itself in a supernova whose light was visible during the day, as documented by multiple civilizations around the world. Its leftover shell of gas and dust has been expanding ever since, and the bright glow is still visible thanks to what remains of the progenitor star: a rapidly spinning neutron star, known as a pulsar. The “crab” moniker stems from a drawing made by the William Parsons, Earl of Rosse, in the early 1840s with a 36-inch telescope, which depicts crab-leg-like appendages, although he later noted that observations through a 72-inch resulted in a view that looked rather different than his original drawing.

Pulsars are some of the most extreme objects in the universe. The Crab Pulsar, which is approximately 12–17 miles (20–28 kilometers) in diameter, spins at a breakneck 30 times per second — once every 33 milliseconds. At magnitude 16.6, it is a very difficult catch, but possible in large (20-plus-inch) scopes on nights with steady skies. It sits only a few arcseconds from a slightly brighter magnitude 15.8 star that guides the way. The pulsar produces a relativistic-speed stellar wind that generates synchrotron radiation, which occurs when charged particles move along curved paths, bent by strong magnetic fields. This is seen across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, forming the main diffuse part of the nebula’s emission. This radiation has a total luminosity some 100,000 times greater than the Sun’s! The pulsar is slowing down gradually as a result of energy carried away by its stellar wind, increasing its period by 36 nanoseconds per day.

The nebula is still expanding, even nearly 1,000 years later, at a rate of 3.4 million mph (5.5 million km/h) — that’s 950 miles (1,527 km) per second, or 0.5% the speed of light! While not noticeable in a single observation, comparing images across several years shows the expansion on very human-accessible timescales.

The Crab’s intricate filaments are what make it so visually stunning in images. These structures are the remnants of the star’s atmosphere, consisting of gases like ionized helium, hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron, neon, and sulfur. It’s a moderately tricky astrophotography target to process: In wideband, it has a largely gray interior wrapped in red tendrils, so it is best imaged in narrowband, where it can display incredible, intricate detail that looks well and truly alien. A famous colorful 2005 Hubble image uses narrowband light from oxygen and sulfur and has oxygen-III set as red, sulfur-II as green, and oxygen-I as blue. When I’ve shot the Crab, I used hydrogen-alpha as blue, since it is a similar wavelength to oxygen-I (which are both red in reality) to create an image reminiscent of the Hubble one, much to my delight.

Whether you are a primarily visual astronomer or a high-tech shutterbug like me, the Crab Nebula is worth spending a little time with this month. Take a moment during your observing to realize how incredible this object is. Rising in the evening hours, it will be up all night for you to enjoy. How much detail can you tease out? Can you spot the pulsar?

Molly Wakeling is an avid astrophotographer active in STEM outreach. She has a Ph.D. in nuclear engineering.

By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have unraveled the workings of a rare disease by putting a large chunk of human DNA into a lab mouse.

The incurable disorder, called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), mostly affects men of Filipino descent and leads to early death. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment.

The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells.

"This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow, an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons.

The two studies, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Cell, not only shed new light on this rare disease but also showcase a powerful technique for mimicking human conditions in laboratory animals. Known as "SwAP-In," it enables researchers to rewrite large portions of an organism's genetic code by inserting big chunks of synthetic DNA. In this case, the approach was used to insert a human gene into lab mice.

"It is kind of a generic method that can be used to make extensively humanized mice," said study co-author Jef Boeke, director of the Institute for Systems Genetics at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a lead developer of the SwAP-In technique.

Liddelow anticipates that this new method for humanizing mice, or tweaking their biology to more closely match that of humans, will prove useful for studying a wide range of diseases, from common conditions like Alzheimer's to "orphan" diseases like XDP, which are rare, underresearched and lacking effective treatments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

XDP is a neurodegenerative condition that particularly impacts the striatum, part of the brain that's crucial for movement. The disease causes symptoms such as slowed movements, tremors, muscle stiffness and involuntary muscle contractions.

On average, symptoms emerge around age 39 and patients live for 13 to 16 years after their symptoms appear. In late stages of the disease, problems with breathing and swallowing can lead to deadly complications such as malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Historically, XDP has also carried a lot of social stigma, which has contributed to high rates of depression and suicide among those with the condition.

"Patients get sort of shunned and hidden away," Liddelow said. That, among other factors, made XDP difficult to study.

XDP shows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (depicted above).

Although XDP isn't fully understood, its underlying genetic cause is known. It stems from a mutation in TAF1, a gene on the X chromosome that helps translate DNA sequences into new proteins. Because males carry only one X chromosome — and thus have no backup copy of the gene — the condition affects far more males than females.

The mutation first appeared in a person on Panay, an island in the Philippines. Due to a phenomenon called the "founder effect," it has risen in prevalence among people of Filipino ancestry but is not seen in other demographics, Boeke explained. Studies suggest there are about 5.7 cases per 100,000 people in the Philippines.

XDP's rarity and associated stigma have made the condition difficult to study, but there's another layer of complexity: The mutation in TAF1 was originally caused by a "jumping gene" ‪—‬ a bit of DNA that changed its position within the genome. In this instance, the DNA happened to jump into the middle of TAF1 and disrupted its function, Boeke said.

But the jumping gene in question is found only in primates. Ideally, if you wanted to study the disease in lab mice, you'd have to insert that jumping gene into their DNA — and that's exactly what the researchers did in the first of their two new studies.

Using SwAP-In, the team inserted 78,000 "letters" of human DNA code into mouse embryonic stem cells. This code included part of the human version of the TAF1 gene and the relevant jumping gene that causes XDP. In both lab dishes and living mice, this gene insertion triggered the telltale signs of XDP: low levels of the TAF1 protein, cell death and holes in the brain, especially in the striatum.

One big difference between mice and humans is that the mouse version of XDP progresses very quickly, with symptoms appearing in just 1.5 months, whereas the human disease takes years to show up. That may be because human bodies have safeguards to help offset the jumping gene's effects — at least for a while — while mice lack this safety net, the study authors theorized.

That difference in disease progression is actually a "huge advantage" for researchers, Boeke noted. "Because it's so sped up, it's possible to do experiments on therapeutics," he said. For instance, if an experimental drug is successfully fighting the disease, that should be obvious in the mice, whose condition would otherwise progress very quickly.

I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients.

In the second of the team's new studies, they took a closer look at the new mice with XDP, to see how the disorder affected their brain cells. Through a battery of tests, they realized that glial cells known as oligodendrocytes showed dramatic changes in both their overall numbers and their gene activity.

These cells would normally make a fatty insulating material called myelin, which wraps around the outgoing wires of neurons to help them send signals. To see how the cells were faring in the XDP mice, study co-author Priya Prakash, a postdoctoral scholar in Liddelow's lab, used a blue stain to label the cells within the mouse brain tissue.

"Where you would normally see this beautiful blue brain, full of lipid, full of myelin, you essentially see a white brain, with none of this lipid there," Liddelow said. This was especially apparent in the striatum and the prefrontal cortex.

Further experiments revealed that the mutation was preventing oligodendrocytes from fully maturing, and that reduced the amount of myelin made in these parts of the brain. They backed up these findings in brains of people with XDP that had been donated after death.

The researchers think this extensive loss of insulation may leave neurons vulnerable to dying early, Liddelow said. In short, "this is a neurodegenerative disease that may not first be manifesting in neurons themselves," he emphasized. "I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients."

Together, the studies raise several ideas for treating XDP. One treatment could involve cranking up the activity of the TAF1 gene to boost the levels of its related protein. This idea showed promise in experiments with mouse cells in the team's first paper. The second paper points to oligodendrocytes as potential targets for future therapies, and myelin loss as a potential early sign of the disease that might be useful for diagnosis.

There's still much more to learn about the biology of XDP and what types of treatments might reverse the drivers of the disease, Liddelow and Boeke emphasized. But now, other scientists have access to a brand-new mouse model that can help them solve the disease's remaining mysteries.

#6334. Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

At 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

That evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese company Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

On Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch company backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, plans to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

Closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not said what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A launched from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

That night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

The week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between launches from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has said only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

#6333. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”

#6330. The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

When it comes to color and contrast, OLED is king, but a great mini-LED TV can give you a great picture, too, often for an excellent price.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive new display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot new multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

My evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV shows via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot new display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

When TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive new mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

The new display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

The TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

One sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

You’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

The step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

The QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

The TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor issue. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

After skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an update for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

Maybe just as impressive are the issues the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a big surprise.

When it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A big reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That said, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s important to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

All of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of new content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

As for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

In contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other new technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

Both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

The most important connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

WiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

Each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is important for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

If you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

Ryan Waniata is a professional writer, editor, video host, and product reviewer. A musician since childhood, his audio hardware roots go back to his days as a studio engineer in Nashville, TN in 2009. In 2011 he left the studio world to became a full-time journalist, with an emphasis on A/V, including TVs, speakers, headphones, and audio gear of all kinds.
